content.title: About
content.content: Chicken breast is the lean, boneless, skinless portion of a chicken. It is high in protein, low in fat, and a staple in many health‑focused diets. Breast meat can be prepared by grilling, baking, sautéing, boiling, or steaming.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Chicken breast provides about 31 g of protein per 100 g.
Compared with dark meat, breast meat contains less fat and fewer calories.
When cooked properly, the meat stays juicy thanks to its natural moisture.
Chicken is a good source of B‑vitamins, especially niacin (B3) and vitamin B6.
Chicken breast is featured in Asian, Mediterranean, and American cuisines worldwide.

items.title: High‑quality protein
items.content: Protein supports muscle growth, tissue repair, and satiety.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: The low saturated‑fat content makes it suitable for heart‑healthy eating.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: B‑vitamins aid carbohydrate, fat, and protein metabolism and support nervous system function.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: Chicken breast supplies phosphorus, selenium and zinc, important for bones, immunity and antioxidant defense.

items.title: Low glycemic impact
items.content: Consuming chicken breast does not cause rapid spikes in blood glucose.

items.title: Food‑borne illness risk
items.content: Undercooked chicken may contain Salmonella or Campylobacter; cook to an internal temperature of 75 °C.

items.title: Chicken allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to chicken proteins.

items.title: Sodium in processed forms
items.content: Smoked or marinated breast often contains added salt, which can be problematic for hypertension.

items.title: Dryness from overcooking
items.content: Over‑cooking leads to dry texture and loss of nutrients.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Breast can be pan‑seared, baked, grilled, or poached in broth. Marinating in lemon juice, olive oil and herbs adds flavor and tenderness. The skin is usually removed, but some recipes keep it for extra taste and texture.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep fresh chicken breast refrigerated at 0‑4 °C for up to 2 days. Freeze at –18 °C for up to 9 months. Before cooking, check for off‑odors or slimy texture; discard if any signs of spoilage are present.

content.title: About
content.content: Steamed trout retains most of its nutrients, offering a delicate flavor and tender texture. It is a popular choice in diet-friendly cooking because no added fat is required for the steaming process.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Trout belongs to the salmon family and is commonly farmed in freshwater ponds.
Steaming preserves up to 90 % of B‑vitamins, which are easily destroyed by frying.
In the wild, trout feeds on insects and small fish, making it rich in omega‑3 fatty acids.
In Japan, steamed trout is often served with soy sauce and ginger as a cooked alternative to sashimi.
Trout can grow up to 1.5 kg, but commercial production usually harvests fish weighing 300–500 g.

items.title: Rich in omega‑3
items.content: Steamed trout provides EPA and DHA, which support heart and brain health.

items.title: High-quality protein
items.content: Approximately 20 g of protein per 100 g helps maintain muscle mass.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Vitamins B12, B6 and niacin aid metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: Trout supplies selenium, phosphorus and potassium, important for immunity and bones.

items.title: Low in calories
items.content: Steamed trout contains about 120 kcal per 100 g, making it suitable for calorie‑controlled diets.

items.title: Fish allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to trout.

items.title: Heavy‑metal contamination
items.content: Wild trout can accumulate mercury and cadmium; choose reputable sources.

items.title: Foodborne illness
items.content: Improper storage can lead to bacterial growth and food poisoning.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Steamed trout can be served whole, flaked into salads, added to soups, or used in sushi rolls. It pairs well with lemon, dill, olive oil, and light sauces.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep cooked trout refrigerated at 0‑4 °C for up to 2 days. For longer storage, freeze in an airtight bag at –18 °C for up to 3 months. Reheat thoroughly before serving.

content.title: About
content.content: Horchata is a traditional refreshing beverage made from rice, cinnamon, vanilla, and sugar, diluted with water. It is popular in Mexico and Latin America, offering a mild sweet flavor and creamy texture.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Horchata originated in ancient Mexico as a fermented rice drink.
It is traditionally served cold over ice on hot days.
Many variations exist: almond horchata, coconut milk horchata, or spiced with nutmeg.
In the United States horchata is often offered in Mexican restaurants as a non‑alcoholic alternative.
Some regions add corn starch for a thicker consistency.

items.title: Carbohydrate source
items.content: Rice provides a quick source of energy.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: The traditional water‑based version contains virtually no fat.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Rice supplies small amounts of B1, B3, and B6 vitamins that support metabolism.

items.title: Hydration
items.content: The large water component helps maintain the body’s fluid balance.

items.title: Antioxidants from spices
items.content: Cinnamon and vanilla contain polyphenols with antioxidant properties.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Traditional horchata is often sweetened, so people with diabetes should monitor portion size.

items.title: Rice allergy
items.content: Rarely, some individuals may be allergic to rice.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: When a lot of sugar is added, the drink can become calorie‑rich.

items.title: Contamination risk in homemade versions
items.content: Improper storage can lead to bacterial growth, especially if left at room temperature for extended periods.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve horchata chilled, often over ice. It can be added to cocktails, used as a base for fruit smoothies, or paired with desserts such as churros or cakes.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep prepared horchata in the refrigerator in a sealed container for up to 3‑4 days. For longer storage, freeze in portion‑size containers.

content.title: About
content.content: Mung beans (Vigna radiata) are small green legumes widely used in Asian cuisine. When cooked they become tender, mildly sweet, and retain their nutritional value. They are commonly added to soups, salads, porridges, and used as a filling for spring rolls.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Mung beans are one of the oldest cultivated legumes, with cultivation dating back over 5,000 years in India and China.
The seeds can sprout in 1–2 days, producing nutrient‑dense microgreens.
In China, mung beans are often used to make a sweet dessert soup called "sweet mung bean soup."
The beans fix nitrogen in the soil, improving its fertility.
In Japan, boiled mung beans are served as a salted snack called "edamame."

items.title: Rich in plant protein
items.content: One cup of cooked mung beans provides about 14 g of protein, making them an excellent protein source for vegetarians.

items.title: Low glycemic index
items.content: Mung beans raise blood sugar slowly, which is beneficial for diabetes management and weight control.

items.title: Source of dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber supports digestion, promotes satiety, and helps maintain gut health.

items.title: Contains B‑vitamins
items.content: B1, B6, and folate contribute to energy metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Minerals and antioxidants
items.content: Mung beans provide iron, magnesium, potassium, and antioxidants that combat free radicals.

items.title: Legume allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to legumes, including mung beans.

items.title: Phytates
items.content: Phytate content can reduce mineral absorption; soaking and cooking help mitigate this.

items.title: Gas formation
items.content: Legumes can cause bloating in sensitive people; gradual introduction to the diet reduces the effect.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Cooked mung beans can be added to soups, salads, rice dishes, used as a filling for spring rolls, or blended into a dip. They also work well in vegetarian patties or as a base for sauces.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store cooked mung beans in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 4‑5 days. For longer storage, freeze them in portioned bags for up to 3 months. Discard any beans with an off‑smell or signs of spoilage.

content.title: About
content.content: Sweet potato, canned, fat added is a ready‑to‑eat product made from selected sweet potato tubers that are sliced, blanched, packed in glass or metal cans and covered with vegetable oil. It retains the characteristic sweet flavor and tender texture, while the added fat increases caloric value and enhances the absorption of fat‑soluble vitamins.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Sweet potato (batata) belongs to the Convolvulaceae family and is not closely related to regular potato.
Canning with added fat helps preserve a brighter color and richer aroma.
Batata is rich in beta‑carotene, which converts to vitamin A during cooking.
In the United States sweet potatoes are often used in casseroles and pies, while in Japan they appear in sweet desserts.
Canned sweet potato has a long shelf life (up to 2‑3 years) compared with fresh roots.

items.title: Rich in beta‑carotene
items.content: Beta‑carotene is converted to vitamin A, supporting vision, immunity and skin health.

items.title: Source of complex carbohydrates
items.content: Provides a steady release of energy, helping maintain stable blood‑sugar levels.

items.title: Contains dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber aids digestion and promotes a feeling of fullness.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Vitamin B6 and B5 are involved in protein and fat metabolism.

items.title: Added fat improves vitamin absorption
items.content: The vegetable oil in the can helps the body absorb fat‑soluble vitamins A and E more efficiently.

items.title: High caloric density
items.content: Added oil raises the energy content, so portion sizes should be moderated.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Some canned varieties contain salt for flavor; people with hypertension should check the label.

items.title: Allergy to vegetable oils
items.content: Individuals allergic to certain oils (e.g., sunflower) may experience reactions.

items.title: Bacterial contamination if seal is broken
items.content: Bulging, rusted, or damaged cans can harbor pathogens and should be discarded.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Canned sweet potato can be eaten cold in salads, warmed in the microwave or skillet, added to stews, soups and casseroles. It makes a quick side dish or a base for mash.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store unopened cans in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. After opening, transfer the contents to an airtight container and keep refrigerated for 3‑5 days. Discard cans that are bulging, rusty or have compromised lids.
